title: Following another school
hookLine: many scholars allow following another school's view in some cases

lines: A HUSBAND WHO NEVER CAME BACK.
KEEP THE DOOR SHUT, OR OPEN IT?
cards: A question lands on a scholar's desk. A woman's husband left home and never came back. No letter.
No word. No grave. Her family follows the Hanafi school, and in its classical books the answer is hard: she waits a very long time before a judge may declare her free to marry again.

The Maliki books give a judge room to act after a far shorter wait. So the scholar has two answers in front of him, one from his own school and one from a neighbor's. He can keep the door shut, or open it.

teach.b: A Muslim who isn't a jurist usually follows a school. Earlier in this block that had a name, taqlid: trusting a madhhab's method instead of rebuilding the law alone. So can a person step outside it?
The jurists don't give one answer. Some held that once you take a school, you keep to it. Others allow following another school's view in some cases.
Hanafi scholars in South Asia, facing wives left in exactly that limbo, wrote a work that drew on the Maliki position, so a judge could end the marriage and the woman could go on with her life.

teach.h: A DOOR OPENED FOR A NEED.
teach.b: The door was opened for a need, and through a judge, not on a whim.

Some of those who allow it point to a line about fasting in surah two, in Pickthall's words: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Then the warning on the other side of the door.
The jurists have a phrase for picking whichever school's view is lightest, in matter after matter, just because it's lightest: tatabbu' ar-rukhas, chasing the concessions.
And there's a related debate over talfiq, stitching: washing for prayer by one school's rule and praying by another's, so that the whole act might count in no single school.
Some scholars forbid it; some allow it within limits.
In practice, a person with a real difficulty asks someone who knows both schools, and the answer comes with a reason.
Not a hole knocked in the wall. A door, with a frame.

how: Muslims who follow a school usually keep to its rulings, and when a hard case arises some ask a scholar whether another school's view may be followed; some scholars allow it for genuine need and warn against picking the easiest view each time.

o: leaving one's school to found a new school of law
taking another school's view for a real need, with a reason
switching schools whenever another one's rule is easier

games.q: following another school — tap the pairs.
p: picking the lightest view every time
a door opened to the Maliki view

s: every scholar forbids ever following another school's view
some held to one school; others allow following another school's view in some cases.
scholars who allow it also warn against chasing the lightest view
picking the lightest view just because it's lightest has its own name: tatabbu' ar-rukhas, chasing the concessions.
talfiq means stitching together views from different schools
for example, washing by one school's rule and praying by another's. some forbid it; some allow it within limits.

games.q: you're a Hanafi scholar. a woman's husband vanished, and your school's classical books make her wait a very long time. what do you do?
o: tell her to keep waiting, whatever it costs her.
draw on the Maliki view, so a judge can free her.
tell her to pick whichever school she likes best.
games.why: Hanafi scholars in South Asia drew on the Maliki position for these cases: a door opened for a real need, through a judge, with a reason.

practice: Let your breathing slow. Bring to mind a time someone made room for you, a deadline moved, a rule bent, because your situation really was hard, and a time you asked for the easy way only because it was easy.
Hold the two side by side, without judging either; if you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Following another school. Some scholars allow taking another school's view in some cases, for a real need, with a reason, and they warn against chasing whatever is lightest. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: stitching pieces together; in law, combining different schools' views within one act.

carryVoice: Your line: doors between schools. A real need, a real reason, and someone who knows. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you

sources.ref: Ashraf Ali Thanawi, al-Hila al-Najiza (Hanafi recourse to the Maliki view on the missing husband)
